target_customer: City riders paying per ride for dockless electric kick scooters; cities as permit grantors
problem: Short last-mile trips in dense cities had no cheap, reliable option, and early scooter operators were being thrown out of cities for ignoring permit rules.
business_model: Usage-based scooter rental (unlock fee plus per minute), operated under city permits

founders.name: Sanjay Dastoor
previous_startups: Boosted Boards (electric skateboards, later shut down)
founders.background_notes: Named co-founder and CEO in the TechCrunch launch article of 2018-05-17. The YC page lists only Matt Tran. Education not found.

founders.name: Matt Tran
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as co-founder of Skip and Boosted. TechCrunch says he ran marketing at Boosted and has an engineering background.

exit.reason: Filed for Chapter 7 liquidation in August 2021 per Wikipedia citing the San Francisco Chronicle of 2021-08-06. Helbiz had reported an acquisition in December 2020, but a later filing described only a license and app rights arrangement.

competitors.name: Bird
competitors.traction_then: Launched in San Francisco in spring 2018 without a permit, later removed under the city permit law

competitors.name: Lime (LimeBike)
competitors.traction_then: Launched in San Francisco in spring 2018

competitors.name: Spin
competitors.traction_then: Launched in San Francisco in spring 2018

technical_complexity.rationale: Skip designed its own kick scooter hardware and fleet software, which is hard for a small team, but the founders came from Boosted Boards and had hardware experience.

defensibility.rationale: Scooters were widely copied. The only edge was a city permit position, such as the 2018 San Francisco pilot, which was limited and temporary.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Well funded rivals were already deploying scooters in 2018. Skip later sold or leased operating rights to Helbiz in December 2020 and then entered Chapter 7 in 2021.

market_need_then: Strong early demand for dockless scooters in 2018 was visible in the rapid launches by Bird, Lime and Spin, while cities pushed back with permit rules that favored compliant operators.

branding.name_origin: The company began under the YC codename Waybots and rebranded to Skip at its May 2018 funding announcement. No source states why Skip was chosen.
branding.domain_note: Used rideskip.com. The domain now redirects to a HugeDomains listing, so it is for sale.

identity.voice_and_tone: Positioned as the compliant, community oriented operator that follows city rules.

rebrands.why: Not stated; announced together with the seed round.

brand_strength.rationale: A branding review graded the name B and called it flat for a wheeled vehicle. No evidence of merch, fan communities or brand driven growth.

outcome_analysis: Skip raised a $6M seed in May 2018 and a reported $25M Series A a month later, then debt, and won one of two San Francisco scooter permits. Scooter sharing proved capital hungry and highly competitive against Bird, Lime and Spin. The company sold rights to Helbiz at the end of 2020 and filed for Chapter 7 in August 2021. The company did not publish a cause, so the failure factors are inferred from the sector pattern and should be read as likely, not stated.
notes: The Series A of $25M rests on Wikipedia, which cites The Information of 2018-06-12; CB Insights reportedly lists a $75M valuation, which is unverified and not recorded. The $100M debt figure rests on a single Bloomberg headline that says 'said to get'. Seed investors beyond Initialized and SV Angel are unclear. The Helbiz December 2020 deal is described as an acquisition by some outlets and as a license in a later filing, so exit is recorded as shutdown. The YC page lists only Matt Tran; the other founders come from TechCrunch. Failure cause is not public.
